extracted.intended_audience: writers, creative-writing students, dramatists, screenwriters, tabletop storytellers, and writing teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using the 'show, don't tell' technique across fiction, nonfiction, drama, screenwriting, and roleplaying — i.e., how to let readers or audiences experience story through concrete detail, action, and sensory material rather than authorial exposition. Includes recommendations, exceptions, and examples from notable practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow reader to experience, not be told
rubrics_metrics.description: "Allow the reader to experience the story through actions, words, subtext, thoughts, senses, and feelings rather than through the author's exposition, summarization, and description."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use actions, dialogue, sensory detail and subtext so readers draw conclusions themselves instead of the author stating meanings. Applies to nonfiction and all forms of fiction, as well as speech, film and playwriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid authorial-analysis adjectives; describe scenes so readers infer
rubrics_metrics.description: "It avoids adjectives describing the author's analysis and instead describes the scene in such a way that readers can draw their own conclusions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete description of what characters do, sense, and say over adverbial or adjectival summaries of internal states (e.g., don't label a character 'angry' — show clenched fists, terse dialogue, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seize on small details and group them to create a picture (Chekhov)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chekhov: "In descriptions of Nature one must seize on small details, grouping them so that when the reader closes his eyes he gets a picture."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select vivid, specific sensory details (e.g., "a piece of glass from a broken bottle glittered like a bright little star") to evoke an entire scene or mood rather than stating it outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use telling only for events that cannot be acted; keep telling brief (Mark Swan)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Events that have happened in the past, which cannot possibly be acted in the present, must be 'told about.' The telling of them is the only narrative or description that should be in a play. Make the 'telling' as brief and crisp as possible..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For drama and scenes outside the present action, compress exposition into short, efficient telling; whenever possible, convert exposition into scenes that allow actors to perform emotions and relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize important scenes; eliminate the author's registering mind (Percy Lubbock)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lubbock's picture-versus-drama distinction: let the action speak and avoid the author's recording mind; the novelist may add stage directions but should aim to present motion of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, present events as drama (scene and action) that lets readers 'watch' the story rather than listen to the storyteller's summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iceberg Theory / purposeful omission (Hemingway)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a writer of prose knows enough of what he is writing about he may omit things that he knows and the reader...will have a feeling of those things as strongly as though the writer had stated them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit some information deliberately; rely on inference, metaphor, understatement, unreliable narration, and ambiguity to reward careful readers and convey depth beneath surface text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor concrete sensory detail over 'thought' verbs (Palahniuk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Palahniuk recommends banning 'thought verbs' ("Thinks, Knows, Understands, Realizes, Believes, Wants, Remembers, Imagines, Desires […]") in favor of "specific sensory detail: action, smell, taste, sound, and feeling."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace verbs that tell inner states with concrete behavior and sensory description that imply those mental states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use telling strategically; don't show everything (James Scott Bell / Orson Scott Card)
rubrics_metrics.description: "'Show, don't tell' should not be applied to all incidents in a story. Sometimes a writer tells as a shortcut... Showing is essentially about making scenes vivid. If you try to do it constantly, the parts that are supposed to stand out won't, and your readers will get exhausted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance showing and telling: show important, dramatic scenes; tell transitional or less important material to move plot and maintain pace. Showing takes more words; telling covers greater spans of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogue to show information (Yves Lavandier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lavandier argues that one can show with dialogue — e.g., pure dialogue between characters can demonstrate skills, relationships, or background without authorial exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let characters' spoken interaction reveal facts, personality, and competence rather than pausing to summarize or explain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey information by performance in live/story contexts (tabletop roleplaying)
rubrics_metrics.description: In tabletop roleplaying, good dungeon masters convey information by stressing intonation and imagery—they do not merely telegraph it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vocal tone, pacing, evocative imagery and sensory detail to immerse players; avoid overtly telling players what to feel or do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to cultural/contextual limits of 'show, don't tell' (critical commentary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Viet Thanh Nguyen questioned teaching 'show, don't tell' as it may be biased against immigrant writers whose emotional expressions may require telling for readers unfamiliar with their cultural cues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience and cultural difference: sometimes explicit telling is necessary or more effective to communicate emotions or cultural contexts that readers might not infer.
